16 ### How classes are detected 17 18 Tailwind treats all of your source files as plain text, and doesn't attempt to actually parse your files as code in any way. 19 20 Instead it just looks for any tokens in your file that could be classes based on which characters Tailwind is expecting in class names: 21 22 ```jsx 23 // [!code filename:JSX] 24 // [!code word:bg-blue-500] 25 // [!code word:rounded-full] 26 // [!code word:text-white] 27 // [!code word:text-black] 28 // [!code word:font-medium] 29 // [!code word:text-sm\/6] 30 // [!code word:font-sans] 31 // [!code word:bg-black] 32 // [!code word:bg-white] 33 // [!code word:className] 34 // [!code word:function] 35 // [!code word:children] 36 // [!code word:button] 37 // [!code word:shadow] 38 // [!code word:export] 39 // [!code word:colors] 40 // [!code word:color] 41 // [!code word:black] 42 // [!code word:white] 43 // [!code word:const] 44 // [!code word:blue] 45 // [!code word:return] 46 // [!code word:py-1.5] 47 // [!code word:px-2] 48 export function Button({ color, children }) { 49 const colors = { 50 black: "bg-black text-white", 51 blue: "bg-blue-500 text-white", 52 white: "bg-white text-black", 53 }; 54 55 return ( 56 59 ); 60 } 61 ``` 62 63 Then it tries to generate the CSS for all of these tokens, throwing away any tokens that don't map to a utility class the framework knows about. 64 65 ### Dynamic class names 66 67 Since Tailwind scans your source files as plain text, it has no way of understanding string concatenation or interpolation in the programming language you're using. 68 69 {<>Don't construct class names dynamically} 70 71 ```html 72 73
74 ``` 75 76 In the example above, the strings `text-red-600` and `text-green-600` do not exist, so Tailwind will not generate those classes. 77 78 Instead, make sure any class names you’re using exist in full: 79 80 {<>Always use complete class names} 81 82 ```html 83 84 85 86
87 ``` 88 89 If you're using a component library like React or Vue, this means you shouldn't use props to dynamically construct classes: 90 91 Don't use props to build class names dynamically 92 93 ```jsx 94 // [!code filename:JSX] 95 function Button({ color, children }) { 96 return ; 97 } 98 ``` 99 100 Instead, map props to complete class names that are statically detectable at build-time: 101 102 Always map props to static class names 103 104 ```jsx 105 // [!code filename:JSX] 106 function Button({ color, children }) { 107 const colorVariants = { 108 blue: "bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-500", 109 red: "bg-red-600 hover:bg-red-500", 110 }; 111 112 return ; 113 } 114 ``` 115 116 This has the added benefit of letting you map different prop values to different color shades for example: 117 118 ```jsx 119 // [!code filename:JSX] 120 function Button({ color, children }) { 121 const colorVariants = { 122 blue: "bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-500 text-white", 123 red: "bg-red-500 hover:bg-red-400 text-white", 124 yellow: "bg-yellow-300 hover:bg-yellow-400 text-black", 125 }; 126 127 return ; 128 } 129 ``` 130

content.text:
This is expected behavior, not a bug: Tailwind scans source files as plain text and can't resolve `{{ Vite::image('hero.jpg') }}` interpolation at build time, so `bg-[url('{{ ... }}')]` never becomes a valid detected class/URL.

Per `src/docs/detecting-classes-in-source-files.mdx` § "Dynamic class names": "Since Tailwind scans your source files as plain text, it has no way of understanding string concatenation or interpolation... Don't construct class names dynamically... make sure any class names you're using exist in full" (lines 65–76).

Your fix (using an inline `style` attribute) is the correct workaround since the URL is only known at runtime/render-time, not at Tailwind's build-time scan.
